content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** A submodule is a separate repository whose chosen commit is recorded by the superproject. Its URL, initialization and update lifecycle need explicit handling; the superproject does not absorb the submodule’s history as ordinary files.

For **Working with Submodules**, keep the named subtopics in view: What a submodule represents; Adding a submodule; Cloning a project containing submodules; Initializing and updating submodules. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. A superproject records a specific submodule commit, not a copy of all submodule history. The URL and access policy are configured separately.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a disposable repository. If the exercise changes state, check git status and git log before and after; discard the practice directory only after confirming it contains no valuable work.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf web lesson page does not execute arbitrary Git commands. Run commands locally in a disposable repository with a Git version appropriate to your task. Placeholder paths, branches, commit IDs and repository URLs must be replaced with values from that practice repository.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
